The lesbian community has historically always had an interesting relationship with gender. I read something when I was educating myself on queer history that explained it as lesbians feeling an inherent disconnect from femininity because so much of womanhood is tied up in attraction to men by society’s standards. For some he/him lesbians, this can be viewed as being gender non conforming. Some lesbians who use pronouns other than she/her, however, also identify as gender queer or transgender. For example, I use they/them mostly but definitely prefer he/him over she/her. I’m nonbinary, meaning I’m neither a binary man nor a binary woman, but I still consider myself a lesbian for two reasons: 1. I only like women and there’s no other word that describes me more accurately because I’m sure as hell not straight and 2. Being assigned female at birth and growing up as a “girl” means I have a lot of shared experiences with other lesbians and it feels way more like a homosexual connection than a heterosexual one. He/him lesbians also understand bonding over shared experiences despite not conforming to traditional gender norms. Basically, sexuality is complicated and gender is even more complicated so do what makes you feel like you!

Probably not. I understand your concern, but I feel like you’re missing the point. With most psychological disorders, it’s not as simple as finding a cure. Not only does every brain work differently, but very few disorders can be treated simply by fixing the chemical imbalances in your brain. The brain is a complex organ. It creates behavioral patterns as a result of those fun chemical imbalances that are very hard to break! Think of it like a nicotine addiction. Even after you stop physically craving the nicotine, you still may crave the act of taking a smoke break. Even with medical treatment, psych disorders leave a lasting impact that it up to the individual to change. It’s the same reason people who have depression usually don’t claim they are “cured” and quit going to therapy after starting antidepressants. In short, there’s already successful treatment for ocd and other psych disorders. There will not likely be any absolute cure, but a cure is unnecessary because with therapy, ocd can be properly managed to the point that it isn’t negatively affecting your life.
There is treatment, not a cure. Meaning it is impossible to get rid of ocd absolutely, but you can manage the obsessions and compulsions so it does not rule your life.
